posts.author: Abhijeet Singh
posts.html:
Prismatic Alternative: viaSocket vs Prismatic for SaaS Integration Delivery

Prismatic is a well-regarded embedded iPaaS platform built specifically for B2B SaaS companies. If you're evaluating Prismatic alternatives, you're likely in one of two situations: you've hit a pricing or scale threshold, or you need integration delivery capabilities — particularly for AI agents — that map differently to your product architecture.

This comparison covers the five criteria that matter most for a SaaS team choosing integration delivery infrastructure: deployment model, pricing transparency, target customer fit, integration breadth, and AI/MCP readiness. It's written to help you make a grounded decision, not to oversell either product.

What Prismatic Is Built For

Prismatic is purpose-built for B2B SaaS companies that need to deliver integrations to enterprise customers. Its core strengths are:

  • A white-labeled embedded workflow builder embedded in your product
  • Deep support for custom connectors, including a low-code connector builder
  • Enterprise-grade infrastructure with strong support for complex, long-running integration workflows
  • White-glove onboarding and implementation support
  • A marketplace model where your customers can discover and activate integration templates

Prismatic has a track record with B2B SaaS companies that need to deliver integrations to enterprise buyers who have complex, bespoke requirements.

If you need heavy customization per customer, dedicated customer success management, and an enterprise-grade SLA with hands-on support, Prismatic is a serious contender and should stay on your shortlist.

Where Teams Look for Alternatives

Teams typically look for Prismatic alternatives when:

  1. Pricing requires a sales call. Prismatic does not publish pricing. Getting a quote requires a discovery call and sales qualification. For early-stage teams, seed-funded startups, or teams that want to prototype before committing, this is a friction point.

  2. AI agent integration delivery model. Prismatic offers MCP capabilities for AI integration, including an MCP flow server that exposes your deployed integration workflows as tools for AI agents to invoke. But the model is workflow-centric: you build and deploy a flow, then AI agents call it. Teams that need to give an AI agent direct, dynamic access to actions across hundreds of apps — without pre-building a flow for each one — need a different integration delivery architecture.

  3. Speed to production. Enterprise-grade platforms with custom connector builders and white-glove onboarding have implementation timelines to match. Teams that need to ship integration capabilities in weeks rather than quarters look for alternatives with faster self-serve paths.

  4. Transparent self-serve pricing. Growing SaaS teams often need to validate economics before sales engagement.

Five-Criteria Comparison: viaSocket vs Prismatic

1. Deployment Model

Prismatic offers an embedded workflow builder (white-labeled, embedded in your SaaS UI, Enterprise tier), a customer-facing integration marketplace, and a headless API for programmatic integration management. The primary model is workflow-builder-centric: your customers build and configure their own integrations within your product.

viaSocket offers three distinct deployment models:

  • Embedded iPaaS — white-labeled workflow builder embedded in your SaaS, backed by 2,300+ pre-built connectors
  • Actions for AI — AI agent tool-calling across 2,300+ apps, with per-user managed auth
  • Actions via Webhook — backend webhook fires multi-app actions; no UI embedding required

For visual workflow builder delivery to end customers, both platforms compete directly. Prismatic has a longer track record in this model; viaSocket offers it as one of three options.

2. Pricing Transparency

Prismatic does not publish pricing. A sales call is required. This is standard for enterprise platforms targeting B2B SaaS at scale, but it creates friction for early-stage teams and makes cost modeling difficult pre-commitment.

viaSocket Embed pricing is published:

  • Sandbox: $0/month — 25 active users, 25K tasks/month
  • Production: $249/month — 1,000 active users, 1M tasks/month
  • Enterprise: Custom

Overages are $1 per user and $1 per 2,500 tasks. No sales call required to start. Full pricing is at /embed/app-integration.

The main viaSocket automation pricing (separate from Embed) starts at $0/month with 100,000 tasks included. Full details at /pricing.

3. Target Customer Fit

Prismatic is optimized for B2B SaaS companies delivering integrations to enterprise customers. The platform assumes complex, bespoke integration requirements per customer, a dedicated integrations team, and an implementation timeline of weeks to months.

viaSocket is optimized for:

  • SaaS founders and product teams who need integration capabilities without a dedicated integrations team
  • AI-native products (copilots, agents) that need to act on third-party apps
  • Platform engineers who need managed OAuth and multi-tenant integration infrastructure
  • Teams that want to ship and iterate quickly with published pricing

Prismatic's strengths — enterprise support, deep customization per customer, white-glove onboarding — are genuine advantages for the right buyer. If your customers are enterprises with complex, negotiated integration requirements, Prismatic is worth the sales conversation.

If your customers are SMBs or mid-market, or if you're building a product where integrations need to be mostly self-serve and low-touch, viaSocket's model is likely a better fit.

4. Integration Breadth

Prismatic supports pre-built connectors (their Component Library) across common B2B categories, plus a low-code connector builder for custom integrations. The emphasis is on quality and configurability per connector rather than breadth.

viaSocket provides 2,300+ pre-built app integrations maintained by the platform — CRM, marketing, support, finance, HR, developer tools, communication, and more. You add them to your product; you don't build or maintain them. See /features for the integration catalog.

For teams whose customers use a wide, unpredictable variety of apps, breadth matters. For teams whose customers use a predictable set of enterprise tools with complex configuration requirements, Prismatic's connector depth may matter more.

5. AI/MCP Readiness

Both platforms offer AI and MCP integration capabilities, but the underlying delivery model is different — and that difference matters depending on what you're building.

Prismatic has invested significantly in AI for integrations. Their platform offers two distinct MCP capabilities: an MCP dev server that connects AI coding assistants (Claude, Cursor) to Prismatic inside a developer's IDE, accelerating how integration workflows are built; and an MCP flow server that exposes your deployed integration workflows as structured tools that your customers' AI agents can discover and invoke at runtime. They also provide built-in connectors for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, LangChain, and other AI services. MCP server support is included from the Scale plan.

The model is workflow-centric: a developer builds and deploys a Prismatic integration flow, and then an AI agent can call that flow via the MCP flow server. This gives you tight control over execution logic, error handling, and business rules inside each tool the AI can invoke.

viaSocket takes a different architectural approach with three distinct AI delivery patterns:

  • Actions for AI — exposes 2,300+ individual app actions as tool calls for your AI agent, with per-user managed OAuth. The agent calls actions directly; no pre-built flow is required for each action.
  • White-label MCP endpoint — a user-facing MCP server your customers can connect their own AI clients to, surfacing your product's integrations as an MCP endpoint.
  • Actions via Webhook — a backend webhook model for triggering multi-app actions without any UI or AI client layer.

The practical distinction: if you need to give an AI agent dynamic, on-demand access to actions across a wide catalog of apps without the overhead of pre-authoring a flow for each integration, viaSocket's direct-action model fits that pattern. If your AI agents should call reliable, pre-defined integration workflows with structured business logic you control, Prismatic's MCP flow server is designed for that.

Neither model is universally superior — they reflect different trade-offs between control and flexibility.

Summary: Which to Choose

Criterion Prismatic viaSocket
Deployment model Workflow builder (Enterprise) + marketplace Workflow builder + AI actions + Webhook
Pricing transparency Sales required Published, starts free
Target customer size Enterprise B2B SaaS SMB to enterprise SaaS + AI products
Integration breadth Curated connectors + custom builder 2,300+ pre-built
AI/MCP readiness MCP server support (Scale+); MCP flow server exposes deployed workflows as AI tools Multi-modal: tool-calling endpoint, white-label MCP endpoint, webhook — no pre-built flow required
Embedded workflow builder Enterprise tier only Available on all Embed plans
White-glove onboarding Strong Limited
Self-serve path Limited Strong

Choose Prismatic if: You're selling to enterprise customers with complex, bespoke integration requirements; your team has implementation capacity; and you need white-glove support and customer success management as part of the vendor relationship. If your AI agents need to call tightly controlled, pre-defined integration workflows with deterministic business logic, Prismatic's MCP flow server is purpose-built for that.

Choose viaSocket if: You need transparent self-serve pricing, a wide pre-built integration catalog, or a faster path from prototype to production. If your AI agent needs dynamic access to actions across a broad set of apps without pre-building a flow for each integration, viaSocket's Actions for AI model is the better fit.

The Embed Sandbox is free: $0/month, 25 active users, 25K tasks — enough to prototype a complete embedded integration experience.

posts.description: Merge.dev is built for unified data models across HRIS, ATS, and CRM. If you need embedded integration UI, AI agent tool-calling, or full API access without schema constraints, here are the best alternatives.
posts.author: Abhijeet Singh
posts.html:
viaSocket is the best Merge.dev alternative for teams building embedded integration UI or AI agent tool-calling into their SaaS product. If you need a unified data model across HRIS, ATS, or CRM categories, Merge remains a strong choice — but if you need full API access, per-customer connection management, or an embedded workflow builder your users can interact with, alternatives give you more.

What Merge.dev is built for

Merge is a unified API platform. You integrate once with Merge and get normalised read/write access across categories: HRIS (Workday, BambooHR, Rippling), ATS (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby), CRM (Salesforce, HubSpot), accounting (QuickBooks, NetSuite), ticketing, and file storage. The value is the normalised schema — your code works the same way regardless of which specific tool your customer uses.

Merge has been repositioning toward AI use cases. Merge Agent Handler claims 5,000+ tools and is designed to give AI agents structured access to business data. Merge Gateway handles routing and observability. These are separate products from Merge Unified, which starts at $650/mo and requires a sales conversation.

Where Merge falls short

Merge's normalised model is also its constraint. You get Merge's schema, not the full API surface of the underlying app. If your use case requires actions or fields outside Merge's model, you have to wait for Merge to support them or work around the abstraction.

Merge does not offer an embedded integration UI. Your users cannot build or manage their own workflows inside your product using Merge. You get data sync and read/write via unified schema — not a builder experience.

If you need AI agents to call arbitrary actions across apps (send a Slack message, create a Jira ticket, update a HubSpot deal), that falls under Merge Agent Handler — a separate product with separate pricing.

Best alternatives to Merge.dev

viaSocket

viaSocket is an Integration Layer for SaaS products and AI agents. It gives your product access to 2,300+ app integrations (source: viasocket.com) without building OAuth, token storage, or API clients yourself.

Where it differs from Merge: viaSocket does not normalise data across categories. You get direct access to each app's API surface through managed auth and action execution. Your code calls the actual Salesforce fields, the actual HubSpot endpoints — not a unified schema.

Three things viaSocket covers that Merge does not:

Embedded integration UI. Your users can build and manage their own integration workflows inside your product using viaSocket's embedded iPaaS. No category constraint, no schema abstraction.

AI agent tool-calling. Actions for AI gives your agent access to 2,300+ app actions with per-user OAuth, connection state management, and runtime execution — embedded directly in your SaaS.

Managed auth for any app. Managed Auth handles OAuth, token refresh, reauthorisation, multi-account, and multi-auth-method per customer across 2,300+ apps.

Pricing: Free Sandbox plan up to 25 active users and 25K tasks/month. Production at $249/mo for up to 1,000 active users and 1M tasks/month. Enterprise pricing available.

Choose viaSocket if: you need embedded integration UI your users interact with, AI agent tool-calling without schema constraints, or managed OAuth across a broad set of apps.

Choose Merge if: you need normalised read/write data sync across HRIS, ATS, CRM, or accounting categories with a single unified schema.

Paragon

Paragon is an embedded iPaaS focused on SaaS-to-SaaS integration workflows. It supports a visual workflow builder your users can interact with and offers managed auth. Paragon has a BAA available (HIPAA) and self-hosting as an option — both genuine advantages over viaSocket at the time of writing.

Paragon's ActionKit provides server-side AI agent tool-calling. Pricing requires a sales conversation for paid tiers.

Choose Paragon if: you need self-hosting, a HIPAA BAA, or a mature embedded iPaaS with a long integration track record.

Composio

Composio is tool-calling infrastructure for AI agents, with 1,660+ toolkits (source: composio.dev/toolkits). It is designed for single-agent, single-developer use cases — connecting your LangChain, CrewAI, or custom agent to third-party APIs.

Composio's Pro plan is $29/mo, which includes $29 in usage credits. Beyond those credits, you pay per tool call. It is not designed for multi-tenant SaaS where each of your customers has their own connected accounts.

Choose Composio if: you are building a single AI agent that needs fast access to pre-built tool integrations and you are not building a multi-tenant SaaS product.

Nango

Nango is open-source managed auth and integration infrastructure. It handles OAuth for 1,000+ APIs and provides pre-built syncs and actions. It is self-hostable and has transparent usage-based pricing: $50/mo which includes $50 in usage credits, then $0.29/connection and $0.72/compute hour beyond that (source: nango.dev/pricing).

Nango does not offer an embedded integration UI for end-users. It is developer infrastructure, not a user-facing builder.

Choose Nango if: you want open-source managed auth infrastructure you can self-host or inspect, and you are comfortable building the integration UI yourself.

Comparison table

viaSocket Merge Paragon Composio Nango
App coverage 2,300+ Unified model (HRIS, ATS, CRM, accounting) 100+ integrations 1,660+ toolkits 1,000+ APIs
Normalised data model No Yes No No No
Embedded integration UI Yes No Yes No No
AI agent tool-calling Yes (Actions for AI) Yes (Agent Handler) Yes (ActionKit) Yes (primary) No (build yourself)
Managed auth Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes
Self-hosting No No Yes No Yes
Public pricing Yes No No Yes Yes

FAQ

Does viaSocket replace Merge for HRIS or ATS data sync?

No. Merge's core value is its normalised schema across HR, recruiting, CRM, and accounting systems. viaSocket gives you direct API access with managed auth — it does not normalise data across categories. If you need unified read/write across HRIS platforms with a single schema, Merge is purpose-built for that.

Can viaSocket handle multi-tenant OAuth the way Merge does?

Yes. viaSocket's Managed Auth isolates OAuth connections per customer. Each of your users has their own connected accounts, token storage, and reauthorisation flow. This is the same isolation model that Merge provides for its category connectors.

What is Merge Agent Handler and how does it compare to viaSocket's Actions for AI?

Merge Agent Handler is Merge's product for AI agent tool-calling, claiming 5,000+ tools. It gives agents structured access to business data via Merge's unified model. viaSocket's Actions for AI gives agents direct action execution across 2,300+ apps without a normalised schema layer — more breadth, less structure. The right choice depends on whether schema normalisation matters for your agent's use case.

Is there a free way to try viaSocket?

Yes. The Sandbox plan is free for up to 25 active users and 25K tasks/month. No credit card required to start.

posts.html:
viaSocket is the best Nango alternative for SaaS teams that need more than managed OAuth — specifically, an embedded integration UI your users can interact with, AI agent tool-calling, or access to more than 1,000 APIs for auth connections. Nango is excellent open-source infrastructure for developers who want managed auth and pre-built syncs; if that scope fits your needs, it may be all you need.

What Nango is built for

Nango is open-source managed auth and integration infrastructure for developers. It handles OAuth for 1,000+ APIs, stores and refreshes tokens, and provides pre-built syncs and actions against those APIs. You can self-host Nango or use the cloud version.

Nango's pricing is usage-based: $50/mo which includes $50 in usage credits, then $0.29/connection and $0.72/compute hour beyond that (source: nango.dev/pricing). There is no flat per-connection subscription — you pay for what you use once your included credits are spent.

Nango advertises 10k+ pre-built tools, triggers, and syncs across those APIs. For auth connections specifically, the comparable figure is 1,000+ APIs supported.

Where Nango falls short

Nango is developer infrastructure — it is not an embedded integration UI your end-users can interact with. If you want your customers to build and manage their own integration workflows inside your product, you need to build that layer on top of Nango yourself.

Nango does not have AI agent tool-calling as a first-class product. It provides the auth and sync primitives that could underpin tool-calling, but you assemble those into an agent tooling layer yourself.

Nango's self-hosting option is a genuine advantage for teams with strict data residency requirements. If that is not a constraint for you, it is architecture complexity you carry.

Best alternatives to Nango

viaSocket

viaSocket is an Integration Layer for SaaS products and AI agents, with 2,300+ app integrations (source: viasocket.com). It covers the same managed auth problem Nango solves, and adds an embedded integration UI, AI agent tool-calling, and a webhook-to-multi-app action layer on top.

Embedded integration UI. The embedded iPaaS puts a visual workflow builder inside your SaaS. Your users connect their apps and set up automations without leaving your product.

AI agent tool-calling. Actions for AI gives your AI agent access to 2,300+ app actions with per-user OAuth isolation and runtime execution, embedded directly in your product.

Managed auth at scale. Managed Auth handles OAuth, token refresh, reauthorisation, multi-account, and multi-auth-method per customer — across 2,300+ apps, compared to Nango's 1,000+ for auth coverage.

On breadth: viaSocket's 2,300+ auth connections is a meaningful lead over Nango's 1,000+ for auth coverage specifically. Nango's 10k+ pre-built tools/triggers/syncs figure covers a different dimension (pre-built data operations) that viaSocket does not claim an equivalent count for.

Pricing: Free Sandbox up to 25 active users and 25K tasks/month. Production at $249/mo for up to 1,000 active users and 1M tasks/month.

Choose viaSocket if: you need embedded integration UI, AI agent tool-calling, or managed auth across more than 1,000 apps without building the user-facing layer yourself.

Choose Nango if: you want open-source, self-hostable managed auth infrastructure you can inspect and extend, and you are comfortable building the integration UI yourself.

Merge

Merge is a unified API platform providing normalised read/write access across HRIS, ATS, CRM, accounting, ticketing, and file storage. Merge Agent Handler extends this to AI agent tool-calling with 5,000+ claimed tools.

Where it differs from Nango: Merge normalises data across categories (Nango does not). You write to Merge's schema, not to individual app APIs. This is powerful for cross-category data sync; it is a constraint when you need full API surface access.

Merge Unified starts at $650/mo and requires a sales conversation. Merge Agent Handler is a separate product with separate pricing.

Choose Merge if: you need normalised read/write data sync across HR, recruiting, CRM, or accounting systems.

Composio is AI agent tool-calling infrastructure with 1,660+ toolkits (source: composio.dev/toolkits). It is built for single-agent, single-developer use cases — plug your LangChain or CrewAI agent into third-party apps quickly.

Composio's Pro plan is $29/mo, which includes $29 in usage credits, then per-call pricing beyond that. It is not designed for multi-tenant SaaS products where each customer has isolated connected accounts.

Choose Composio if: you are building a single AI agent and want fast access to pre-built tool integrations without building a multi-tenant auth layer.

Workato

Workato is an enterprise integration and automation platform. It covers embedded iPaaS, API management, and workflow automation at scale. It does not publish pricing — you engage sales for a quote.

Choose Workato if: you are at enterprise scale, need deep workflow orchestration, and have budget for a premium platform with sales support.

Pipedream Connect

Pipedream Connect provides managed OAuth and action execution across 2,000+ apps, with an API designed for developers building auth flows into their SaaS product. It is developer-first and does not include an embedded visual workflow builder for end-users.

Choose Pipedream Connect if: you want a developer-focused managed auth and action API and are comfortable without an embedded UI.

No. viaSocket runs on Google Cloud Platform (GKE) and is cloud-only. If data residency or self-hosting is a hard requirement, Nango's self-hosted option is a genuine advantage.

posts.title: Embedded iPaaS Comparison: viaSocket vs Paragon vs Prismatic vs Composio
posts.description: A detailed comparison of the top embedded iPaaS platforms — viaSocket, Paragon, Prismatic, and Composio — covering app count, pricing, MCP support, AI agent tool-calling, and embed options.
posts.author: Abhijeet Singh
posts.category: CL-2 — Embedded iPaaS & Integration Layer for SaaS Builders
posts.html:
Choosing an embedded iPaaS platform is a significant infrastructure decision. The platform you pick handles OAuth for your users, stores their credentials, executes their integrations, and sits in the critical path of your product. Getting it wrong means a costly migration later.

This comparison covers four platforms — viaSocket, Paragon, Prismatic, and Composio — across the dimensions that matter most to SaaS engineering teams: app coverage, pricing model, embed options, AI agent support, MCP capabilities, security posture, and developer experience.

What Is Embedded iPaaS?

An embedded iPaaS (Integration Platform as a Service) is integration infrastructure you embed inside your own SaaS product. Instead of your users leaving your product to configure integrations in a third-party tool, the integration UI and logic live inside your product — under your brand.

The platform handles the hard parts: OAuth flows, token storage and refresh, API clients for hundreds of apps, error handling, and retry logic. Your team ships the integration experience; the platform provides the plumbing.

The Four Platforms

viaSocket

viaSocket is positioned as an Integration Layer for SaaS products and AI agents. It provides a developer API to connect, authenticate, and act on 2,300+ apps, plus three embed products:

  • /embed/app-integration: a visual workflow builder your users run inside your product
  • /embed/actions-for-ai: a tool-calling endpoint for AI agents, backed by 2,300+ apps
  • /embed/actions-via-webhook: webhook-triggered multi-app actions

viaSocket also offers white-label MCP server infrastructure for SaaS companies, letting your users connect their AI assistants (Claude, Cursor) to your product via MCP.

Pricing: Sandbox $0 (25 active users, 25K tasks/month), Production $249/month (1,000 active users, 1M tasks/month), Enterprise custom. Overage: $1/user, $1/2,500 tasks.

Security: SOC 2 Type II certified, ISO certified, GDPR and CCPA compliant, 99.99% uptime SLA, HTTPS behind Cloudflare with DDoS protection.

Paragon

Paragon is an embedded iPaaS focused on SaaS companies. It provides a visual workflow builder, Connect (embedded auth UI), and ActionKit (its AI agent integration layer with MCP server support). Paragon targets enterprise SaaS and has pricing that requires contacting sales for exact rates, with a self-serve start available on its website.

App coverage: Paragon supports a catalog of pre-built integrations; exact count is not prominently stated in public documentation. MCP support is available via ActionKit, positioned primarily for giving your SaaS's AI agent access to third-party integrations.

Prismatic

Prismatic is an embedded iPaaS aimed at B2B SaaS companies. It provides an embedded integration marketplace, a low-code integration designer, and support for custom connectors. Prismatic's connector count is listed as 1,000+ per viaSocket's comparison data — Prismatic does not prominently state a total connector count in its public-facing documentation, so this figure should be treated as an approximation and verified directly with Prismatic for procurement decisions.

Prismatic pricing is not publicly listed; it requires contacting sales.

Composio

Composio is positioned as an AI agent tooling platform with a large toolkit catalog (1,500+ tools as of live pricing data, 2026-10-25). It is primarily designed for AI agent developers who need pre-built tool definitions for external services. Composio has an embed offering, but its primary positioning and developer experience are optimized for AI/LLM use cases rather than SaaS workflow automation.

How to Read the App / Tool Count

Raw app counts are an imperfect proxy for integration quality. A platform with 2,300+ integrations is more useful than one with 500 only if the specific apps your users need are covered and the actions available for those apps match your use case.

Before finalizing a platform choice, verify:

  1. Your top 10 user-requested integrations are available — not just the app logo, but the specific actions (read, write, trigger) your users need.
  2. The integration is maintained — check when it was last updated and whether the platform has a process for keeping integrations current as upstream APIs change.
  3. Custom connectors are possible — for long-tail integrations specific to your users' stack, you need a path to build and maintain custom connectors without rebuilding the entire auth and execution infrastructure.

AI Agent and MCP Support: What to Evaluate

AI agent integration is the fastest-moving dimension in this space. All four platforms are expanding their AI capabilities, but they approach it differently.

Tool-calling endpoints (your AI agent calls the platform to act on third-party apps) are table stakes at this point. The key questions are: what is the latency, what is the error handling model, and how do you control which tools are available to which agents?

White-label MCP (your users connect their AI client to your product via MCP) is a distinct capability. This is about giving your users a branded MCP endpoint they configure in Claude, Cursor, or another MCP client. Evaluate: is the endpoint truly user-facing and white-labeled to your brand, or is MCP used internally by the platform's own tooling?

viaSocket's white-label MCP for SaaS provides a user-facing branded MCP endpoint. Its Embed Actions for AI handles the AI agent tool-calling side.

Pricing Model Considerations

Embedded iPaaS pricing structures vary significantly and the sticker price rarely tells the full story.

Task-based pricing (viaSocket): you pay per integration action executed. Predictable at low volume; model your expected task volume against the tier limits before committing.

User-based pricing (viaSocket Embed also has a user component): you pay per active user with connected integrations. Works well when your user base is well-defined; watch for overage costs if usage spikes.

Sales-required pricing (Paragon, Prismatic): the platform requires a sales conversation before you get a number. Factor in the time cost and the fact that pricing may be negotiated, not fixed.

Usage-based pricing (Composio): can be cost-effective at low volume, less predictable at scale.

viaSocket's Production tier at $249/month covers 1,000 active users and 1M tasks/month. Overage is $1/user and $1/2,500 tasks. Enterprise pricing is custom.

Developer Experience

Embedded iPaaS platforms differ significantly in how much they ask of your engineering team.

viaSocket provides an npm SDK (viasocket-apps) with zero dependencies, supporting Node 20+, Bun, Deno, and edge runtimes under MIT license. Auth uses JWT HS256 signed with org_id, project_id, and embed_secret. The developer docs are at /developers/docs.

Paragon provides SDKs for common frameworks. Integration setup is primarily done through a visual designer with code steps available.

Prismatic provides a component SDK and a visual designer. Custom connector development requires more upfront investment but gives more control.

Composio is optimized for AI/LLM developers; its SDK and documentation are oriented toward agent frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI) rather than SaaS embedding.

Which Platform Fits Which Team

Choose viaSocket if: you want a single Integration Layer for both embedded iPaaS and AI agent tool-calling, need a public pricing starting point without a sales call, and want white-label MCP server support alongside traditional workflow embedding.

Choose Paragon if: you are an enterprise SaaS company with a dedicated integrations team and need a mature embedded integration marketplace with strong enterprise sales support.

Choose Prismatic if: you are a B2B SaaS company with complex, customer-specific integration requirements and the engineering capacity to build and maintain custom connectors.

Choose Composio if: your primary use case is AI agent tooling (giving LLM-based agents access to external tools) rather than embedding workflow automation inside a SaaS product UI.

Summary

All four platforms can handle the core embedded integration requirement — managed OAuth, multi-app connectivity, embedded UI. The differentiation is in AI agent support, MCP capabilities, pricing transparency, and how much engineering investment each requires.

viaSocket's Integration Layer covers the full stack: embedded iPaaS, AI agent tool-calling, and white-label MCP — with public pricing that lets you start evaluating without a sales call.

What is the difference between embedded iPaaS and a native integration?

A native integration is built and maintained entirely by your engineering team — you write the API client, handle OAuth, manage token refresh, and keep the integration current as the upstream API changes. An embedded iPaaS provides that infrastructure as a platform; you configure and embed the integration experience, the platform handles the plumbing.

Yes, if the platform supports it. viaSocket's Embed Actions for AI provides a tool-calling endpoint backed by 2,300+ app integrations specifically for AI agents. Not all embedded iPaaS platforms have a mature AI agent offering.

What is white-label MCP and do I need it?

A white-label MCP server lets your users connect their AI assistants (Claude, Cursor) to your product by pasting an MCP endpoint URL into their AI client. You need it if your users are operating from AI clients and want to invoke your product's features from there. If your users configure integrations inside your product's UI, you need embedded iPaaS. Many products will eventually want both.

How do I evaluate app coverage beyond the headline count?

Check whether your users' most-requested apps are supported, verify the specific actions available (not just the app connection), and confirm the integration is actively maintained. A smaller catalog with well-maintained integrations is more useful than a large catalog with stale ones.

posts.title: How to Add Managed OAuth for Third-Party Apps to Your Product
posts.description: Learn how to add managed OAuth for third-party apps to your SaaS product using viaSocket's managed auth layer — JWT signing, SDK setup, per-user credential isolation, and action execution across 2,300+ apps.
posts.author: Abhijeet Singh
posts.html:
You add managed OAuth for third-party apps by signing a JWT on your backend and passing it to a managed auth SDK that handles every OAuth flow, token storage, and refresh on behalf of each user. viaSocket's managed auth layer covers 2,300+ apps with this model, so your team never builds or maintains individual OAuth clients.

What "managed OAuth" actually means

Managed OAuth means a third-party service owns the OAuth infrastructure while your product owns the user experience. You do not register OAuth apps with each provider, implement authorization code flows, store refresh tokens, or handle provider-specific token expiry behaviour. The managed layer does all of that. Your code contributes one thing: a stable identifier for each of your users so the managed layer can scope credentials correctly.

This is distinct from Auth0, Clerk, or similar identity tools. Those handle how your users log in to your product. Managed OAuth for third-party apps handles how your users' accounts at Slack, HubSpot, Salesforce, Notion, Stripe, and thousands of other services connect to your product after they are already logged in.

Why building OAuth yourself is the wrong default

Most teams discover the cost of DIY OAuth integration after the first three or four connectors. The initial implementation is tractable. The maintenance burden is not.

Each OAuth provider has different token lifetimes, refresh behaviour, and scope models. Google tokens expire in one hour and can be revoked silently. Slack tokens last indefinitely but can be invalidated by workspace admins. Each provider's error codes for expired or revoked tokens are different. In a multi-tenant product, you also need per-user credential isolation: User A's Slack token must never be retrievable in a request scoped to User B.

Building that yourself requires encrypted token storage, per-user keying, per-provider refresh logic, re-authentication prompts when tokens are revoked, and ongoing updates each time a provider changes its OAuth endpoints or scope requirements. A managed OAuth layer moves all of this off your roadmap.

The four steps to add managed OAuth with viaSocket

viaSocket's managed auth is built around a JWT signing pattern. Your backend signs the token; viaSocket scopes everything to the identifier inside it.

Step 1: Install the SDK

npm install viasocket-apps

The SDK is MIT-licensed, has zero dependencies, and supports Node 20+, Bun, Deno, and edge runtimes.

Step 2: Sign a JWT on your server

import jwt from 'jsonwebtoken';

function generateEmbedToken(userId) {
  const payload = {
    org_id: process.env.VIASOCKET_ORG_ID,
    project_id: process.env.VIASOCKET_PROJECT_ID,
    unique_identifier: userId
  };
  return jwt.sign(payload, process.env.VIASOCKET_EMBED_SECRET, {
    algorithm: 'HS256',
    expiresIn: '1h'
  });
}

Three things to get right here:

  • VIASOCKET_EMBED_SECRET is the HS256 signing key passed as the second argument to jwt.sign(). It is not a field in the payload. Never put it in the payload and never send it to the browser.
  • unique_identifier is your per-user stable ID. Use your internal user ID or tenant ID. Do not use email addresses, which can change.
  • Sign on the server only. Return the token to the frontend via a protected API endpoint.

Step 3: Initialise the SDK on the frontend

import { viasocket } from 'viasocket-apps';

const token = await fetch('/api/embed-token').then(r => r.text());
await viasocket.init({ token });

Once initialised, the SDK renders a connect UI scoped to that user. Your users click to connect any of the 2,300+ supported apps, complete the OAuth flow inside viaSocket's hosted flow, and their token is stored under their unique_identifier.

Step 4: Execute actions against connected apps

After a user connects an app, your backend can act on their behalf without touching a token directly:

const response = await fetch(
  `https://flow.sokt.io/func/${process.env.VIASOCKET_SCRIPT_ID}`,
  {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      unique_identifier: userId,
      app: 'slack',
      action: 'send_message',
      params: {
        channel: '#general',
        text: 'Your export is ready.'
      }
    })
  }
);

No Authorization header. The script_id in the URL is the credential that identifies which workflow to run. Keep script_id values in environment variables.

What viaSocket handles after setup

Once a user connects an app through the flow above, viaSocket manages:

  • Token storage and encryption at rest
  • Refresh token rotation on expiry
  • Provider-specific OAuth edge cases
  • Re-authentication prompts when a token is revoked by the provider

The same pattern works across all 2,300+ supported apps. You do not write any provider-specific code.

How this compares to building it yourself

The managed OAuth approach trades implementation control for speed and maintenance relief. A few tradeoffs to understand before choosing it:

Vendor dependency. Your credential storage is on viaSocket's infrastructure. Evaluate the security posture (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001:2022, AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.2+ in transit) and the SLA (99.99% uptime) before committing for production workloads.

App coverage vs. custom connectors. 2,300+ apps covers the long tail for most SaaS products. For apps not in the catalog, viaSocket provides a Plug Builder path to add custom connectors without rebuilding the auth infrastructure.

Pricing model. viaSocket charges per task (integration action executed) and per active user on the embed tiers. The embed Sandbox tier is free for up to 25 active users and 25,000 tasks per month. Production is $249/month for 1,000 active users and 1M tasks. Overage is $1/user and $1/2,500 tasks.

Alternatives. Nango, Pipedream Connect, Paragon, and Merge take similar approaches with different catalog sizes, pricing structures, and target audiences. The architecture pattern (backend JWT signing, managed token storage, per-user scoping) is consistent across all of them. The differentiators are app coverage, pricing transparency, embed options, and AI agent support.

Multi-tenant credential isolation

In a multi-tenant SaaS product, the unique_identifier field is the isolation boundary. Every credential viaSocket stores is keyed to your org_id, project_id, and unique_identifier together. A request with User A's identifier cannot retrieve User B's tokens. This is enforced at the storage layer, not just at the application layer.

Your responsibility is correct identifier routing on your backend. The identifier in the JWT you sign must match the authenticated user in that session. A backend bug that signs a JWT with the wrong identifier is the only way cross-tenant credential access can occur.

Security checklist before going to production

  • embed_secret is in an environment variable, not in source code
  • embed_secret is the JWT signing key only, not a payload field
  • JWT signing happens on your server, never in browser code
  • script_id values are in environment variables
  • JWT expiry is set to one hour or less
  • unique_identifier maps one-to-one to your user records and is immutable
  • No OAuth tokens are cached in your own database (let viaSocket own storage)

FAQ

Do I need to register OAuth apps with each provider?

No. With managed OAuth, viaSocket maintains the OAuth app registrations with each provider. Your users authorise through those registrations. You do not interact with any provider's developer console for the apps in the catalog.

What happens when a user's token expires?

viaSocket handles refresh token rotation automatically. If a provider revokes a token and refresh is not possible, the platform surfaces a re-authentication event. You can handle this in your frontend by checking connection status and prompting the user to reconnect.

Can I add apps that are not in the 2,300+ catalog?

Yes. viaSocket's Plug Builder lets you define a custom connector for any app with an API. The custom connector uses the same managed OAuth infrastructure as the built-in catalog, so you do not rebuild token storage or refresh logic.

Is this the same as using Auth0 or Clerk for OAuth?

No. Auth0, Clerk, and similar tools handle how your users authenticate to your product (login). Managed OAuth for third-party apps handles how your users' accounts at external services (Slack, HubSpot, Stripe) connect to your product after login. They solve different problems and are typically used together.

How do I handle a user who wants to connect multiple accounts from the same app?

viaSocket's managed auth supports multi-account connections per user per app. The connection management UI lets users connect more than one account (for example, two different Slack workspaces), and the action execution layer lets you reference a specific connection by connection ID.

posts.title: How to Handle OAuth for an AI Agent Acting on a User's Apps
posts.description: An AI agent acting on a user's apps needs managed OAuth that stores credentials per user and scopes every action to the right tokens. This guide covers the correct architecture, implementation steps with viaSocket, and how to handle re-authorisation when tokens expire.
posts.author: Abhijeet Singh
posts.html:
An AI agent acting on a user's apps needs a managed OAuth layer that stores the user's credentials, scopes every action to that user's tokens, and never mixes one user's credentials with another's. viaSocket's managed auth and Actions for AI embed product handle this across 2,300+ apps, so your agent calls a single endpoint rather than implementing OAuth per app.

Why OAuth for AI agents is different from OAuth for humans

When a human authorises an OAuth flow, they are present in the browser and can complete a redirect. An AI agent runs server-side and cannot complete a browser-based OAuth flow on its own. The agent needs the user to authorise access upfront, with credentials stored and retrievable so the agent can act on the user's behalf later, potentially long after the original authorisation.

This creates two distinct phases:

  1. Authorisation phase — the user (a human) connects their apps through a UI. This is a standard OAuth flow that must happen in a browser.
  2. Action phase — the agent acts on the user's behalf using the stored credentials. This is a server-side API call, no browser involved.

Conflating these two phases is the most common architecture mistake in agent OAuth implementations. The agent cannot do phase 1. A managed OAuth layer handles phase 1 for you, so your agent only needs to handle phase 2.

The right architecture for agent OAuth

The correct pattern has four components:

  1. Your backend — signs a per-user JWT to identify which user's credentials to use
  2. A connect UI in your product — lets the user authorise their apps before the agent runs (phase 1)
  3. Stored credentials — managed by the OAuth layer, scoped to the user's identifier
  4. Your agent's action calls — server-side requests that reference the user's identifier to retrieve the right credentials (phase 2)

The agent never touches credentials directly. It calls an endpoint with a user identifier, and the managed layer resolves which tokens to use.

Setting up user authorisation with viaSocket

Before your agent can act on a user's apps, the user connects those apps through a UI you embed in your product. viaSocket's managed auth SDK handles the OAuth flows.

On your backend, sign a JWT per user:

import jwt from 'jsonwebtoken';

function getAgentToken(userId) {
  return jwt.sign(
    {
      org_id: process.env.VIASOCKET_ORG_ID,
      project_id: process.env.VIASOCKET_PROJECT_ID,
      unique_identifier: userId
    },
    process.env.VIASOCKET_EMBED_SECRET,
    { algorithm: 'HS256', expiresIn: '1h' }
  );
}

unique_identifier is your stable per-user ID. It scopes all credential storage for this user. The embed_secret is the HS256 signing key passed as the second argument — it is not in the payload and never leaves your server.

On your frontend, initialise the SDK with that token:

import { viasocket } from 'viasocket-apps';

const token = await fetch('/api/agent-token').then(r => r.text());
await viasocket.init({ token });

// Let the user connect their apps
await viasocket.connect({ app: 'gmail' });
await viasocket.connect({ app: 'notion' });

The user completes each OAuth flow in the viaSocket-hosted flow. Their tokens are stored under their unique_identifier.

How the agent executes actions

Once the user has connected their apps, your agent acts on their behalf by calling viaSocket's action execution endpoint with the user's identifier:

async function agentSendEmail(userId, recipient, subject, body) {
  const response = await fetch(
    `https://flow.sokt.io/func/${process.env.VIASOCKET_SCRIPT_ID}`,
    {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        unique_identifier: userId,
        app: 'gmail',
        action: 'send_email',
        params: { to: recipient, subject, body }
      })
    }
  );
  return response.json();
}

The agent supplies the unique_identifier for the user it is acting on behalf of. viaSocket retrieves that user's Gmail credentials and executes the action. The agent never sees the OAuth token.

This pattern scales to any of the 2,300+ apps in the catalog. The same code structure works whether the agent is sending an email, creating a Notion page, updating a HubSpot contact, or posting to Slack.

Scoping agent permissions correctly

An AI agent acting on a user's apps should only have access to the apps that user has explicitly connected, and only the actions appropriate for your agent's scope. Two properties matter here.

Per-user scoping. The unique_identifier in the action call is the isolation boundary. Credentials stored for User A cannot be retrieved in a call that uses User B's identifier. If your agent handles multiple users, it must pass the correct identifier for each action. A routing bug here is a security incident.

App and action scoping. Before your agent attempts an action, verify the user has connected the relevant app:

const enabled = await viasocket.user.findEnabled();
const hasGmail = enabled.some(app => app.name === 'gmail');

if (!hasGmail) {
  return 'User has not connected Gmail. Ask them to connect it in settings.';
}

This prevents your agent from attempting actions on unconnected apps and gives you a clean path to prompt the user to connect what is needed.

Handling re-authorisation

OAuth tokens expire and get revoked. When a user's token for a connected app is no longer valid, the managed layer surfaces this as a connection status change. Your agent should handle action failures that indicate a broken connection by surfacing a re-authorisation prompt to the user rather than retrying indefinitely.

A pattern that works: catch action failures from viaSocket, check connection status with viasocket.user.findEnabled(), and if the app is no longer showing as connected, return a message to the user asking them to reconnect. The agent cannot re-authorise on the user's behalf — that browser-based flow must involve the user.

Multi-agent and multi-tenant patterns

If your product runs agents for multiple users simultaneously, each agent action must carry the correct unique_identifier for the user it is acting on. There is no shared credential pool. Two users who have both connected Slack each have separate, isolated token records.

In an agentic product with multiple agent types (a scheduling agent, a communications agent, a data agent), all agents acting on behalf of the same user can share the same unique_identifier. The scoping is per-user, not per-agent.

viaSocket's Actions for AI embed product

viaSocket's Actions for AI product is built specifically for the agent use case. It exposes 2,300+ app actions as a tool-calling endpoint. Rather than calling individual app APIs, your agent calls a single endpoint and specifies which app and action it needs. The managed auth layer resolves the user's credentials.

This is distinct from viaSocket's white-label MCP server, which is for giving users a branded MCP endpoint they configure in their AI client (Claude, Cursor). Actions for AI is for your agent making server-side calls. Both can be used in the same product.

Adding managed OAuth for the third-party apps an agent will call is covered in How to Handle OAuth for an AI Agent Acting on a User's Apps.

How OAuth for AI agents compares with Merge Agent Handler is covered in the alternatives guide.

How that tool-calling layer compares with Nango and other API auth platforms is covered in OAuth for AI agents.

How viaSocket compares with Composio for that tool-calling setup is in OAuth for AI agents.

FAQ

Can my AI agent complete the OAuth flow on behalf of the user?

No. OAuth authorisation flows are browser-based and require user interaction. Your agent cannot complete them. The user must connect their apps through a UI before the agent can act on those apps. Build a connect-your-apps step into your product's onboarding or settings.

What if the user has not connected an app the agent needs?

Check connection status before the agent attempts an action. If the app is not connected, surface a prompt asking the user to connect it. Do not attempt the action without a valid connection.

How do I prevent one user's agent from accessing another user's apps?

Use a unique, stable unique_identifier per user in every JWT and action call. viaSocket's managed auth layer scopes all credential storage and retrieval to this identifier at the storage level. As long as your backend routes the correct identifier per user session, cross-user access is not possible.

Does this work with LLM tool-calling frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex?

Yes. The action execution is a standard HTTP POST. You can wrap it as a tool in any framework that supports custom tool definitions. Define a tool that calls flow.sokt.io/func/<script_id> with the appropriate parameters and your agent framework can invoke it like any other tool.

Does viaSocket's managed auth work for agents running on behalf of a user without the user being present?

Yes. Once the user has authorised their apps, the stored credentials are available for your agent to use in background tasks, scheduled runs, or triggered workflows. The user does not need to be active in a session for the agent to act.

posts.title: How to Handle OAuth for Multi-Tenant SaaS Integrations with viaSocket
posts.description: Most SaaS products need dozens of third-party integrations, each with its own OAuth flow, token storage, and per-tenant credential isolation. This guide explains how viaSocket's managed OAuth layer handles all of that, and how to wire it into your backend correctly using JWT and the viasocket-apps SDK.
posts.author: Abhijeet Singh
posts.html:
Most SaaS products eventually need to integrate with third-party apps — a CRM, a ticketing system, a messaging platform. Each integration means an OAuth flow, token storage, refresh handling, and strict per-tenant isolation. Building all of that yourself takes weeks per integration and creates ongoing maintenance risk.

viaSocket's managed OAuth layer handles authentication for 2,300+ apps. Your backend issues a signed JWT, your frontend renders a connect widget, and viaSocket stores and refreshes tokens on behalf of each user. This guide walks through the architecture, the correct JWT signing pattern, and how to execute actions against connected apps.

Why Managed OAuth Matters for Multi-Tenant SaaS

In a multi-tenant SaaS product, every user's credentials must be completely isolated. A bug in credential routing — returning User A's Slack token to a request scoped to User B — is a serious security incident.

Building OAuth yourself requires:

  • Registering an OAuth app with each provider
  • Implementing the authorization code flow per provider
  • Storing, encrypting, and rotating refresh tokens
  • Handling provider-specific token expiry behaviour
  • Ensuring per-tenant isolation throughout

viaSocket's managed OAuth layer moves all of this out of your codebase. You identify each user with a unique_identifier — a stable string from your own system — and viaSocket scopes all credential storage and retrieval to that identifier automatically.

Architecture Overview

The integration layer has three components on your side:

  1. Your backend — signs a JWT using your embed_secret and returns it to your frontend
  2. Your frontend — initialises the viasocket-apps SDK with that JWT to render the connect UI
  3. Your backend (action execution) — calls flow.sokt.io/func/<script_id> to trigger actions against connected apps

Your embed_secret never leaves your server. It is the HS256 signing key — it does not appear in the JWT payload.

Step 1: Generate the JWT on Your Server

Install the SDK:

npm install viasocket-apps

Sign a JWT for each user session on your backend:

import jwt from 'jsonwebtoken';

function generateEmbedToken(userId) {
  const payload = {
    org_id: process.env.VIASOCKET_ORG_ID,
    project_id: process.env.VIASOCKET_PROJECT_ID,
    unique_identifier: userId
  };
  return jwt.sign(payload, process.env.VIASOCKET_EMBED_SECRET, {
    algorithm: 'HS256',
    expiresIn: '1h'
  });
}

Critical: VIASOCKET_EMBED_SECRET is the signing key passed as the second argument to jwt.sign(). It is not a field inside the payload object. Never include embed_secret in the JWT payload, and never send it to the browser.

The three payload fields are:

  • org_id — your viaSocket organisation ID
  • project_id — your viaSocket project ID
  • unique_identifier — your per-user identifier; viaSocket uses this to scope all credential storage

Step 2: Initialise the SDK on the Frontend

Return the signed token to your frontend via a protected API endpoint, then initialise the SDK:

import { viasocket } from 'viasocket-apps';

const token = await fetch('/api/embed-token').then(r => r.text());
await viasocket.init({ token });

Once initialised, you can use the SDK to manage connections for the current user.

Step 3: Manage User Connections

The SDK provides a set of methods for the full connection lifecycle:

// Open the connect UI for a specific app
await viasocket.connect({ app: 'slack' });

// List all apps the user has enabled
const enabled = await viasocket.user.findEnabled();

// Check available connection options for an app
const options = await viasocket.user.listOptions({ app: 'hubspot' });

// Enable a specific connection
await viasocket.user.enable({ app: 'notion', connection_id: '...' });

// Get a short-lived token for the current user
const userToken = await viasocket.user.token();

Each call is automatically scoped to the unique_identifier from the JWT. There is no way for one user's session to access another user's connections through the SDK.

Step 4: Execute Actions Against Connected Apps

Once a user has connected an app, your backend can execute actions using the flow.sokt.io endpoint:

const response = await fetch(
  `https://flow.sokt.io/func/${process.env.VIASOCKET_SCRIPT_ID}`,
  {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      unique_identifier: userId,
      app: 'slack',
      action: 'send_message',
      params: {
        channel: '#general',
        text: 'Integration connected successfully.'
      }
    })
  }
);

Important: There is no Authorization header on this request. The script_id in the URL is itself the credential — it identifies which workflow to run and authorises the call. Keep your script_id values in environment variables and do not expose them to the browser.

Per-Tenant Isolation: How It Works

Every credential viaSocket stores is keyed to the combination of your org_id, project_id, and unique_identifier. When your backend calls flow.sokt.io/func/<script_id> with a given unique_identifier, viaSocket retrieves only the tokens associated with that identifier.

This means:

  • Two users who have both connected Slack get separate, isolated token records
  • A call scoped to User A cannot retrieve User B's tokens
  • Revoking a connection for one user does not affect any other user

Your responsibility is to ensure the unique_identifier you embed in the JWT is stable and maps one-to-one to your own user records. A good choice is your internal user ID or a hashed version of it. Do not use email addresses if they can change.

Security Checklist

Before going to production:

  • embed_secret is stored in an environment variable, never in source code
  • embed_secret is used only as the JWT signing key — it does not appear in the payload
  • JWT generation happens on your server, never in browser-side code
  • script_id values are stored in environment variables
  • No Authorization header is added to flow.sokt.io action calls
  • unique_identifier values are stable and map one-to-one to your user records
  • JWT expiry is set to a short window (1 hour or less) and refreshed via your backend

What viaSocket Handles for You

Once a user connects an app through the SDK:

  • Token storage and encryption
  • Refresh token rotation on expiry
  • Provider-specific OAuth edge cases
  • Re-authentication prompts when a token is revoked

You do not need to implement any of this per-integration. The same pattern works across all 2,300+ supported apps.

posts.title: Multi-Tenant Integration Architecture: How to Build SaaS Integrations That Scale
posts.description: Building integrations into a multi-tenant SaaS product requires credential isolation, per-user routing, and a connection lifecycle that scales with your user base. This guide covers the architecture patterns that keep one tenant's data separate from another's, using viaSocket's Integration Layer as the implementation reference.
posts.author: Abhijeet Singh
posts.html:
Adding integrations to a multi-tenant SaaS product is not the same as adding integrations to a single-user tool. When thousands of tenants each connect their own Slack, HubSpot, or Stripe account, the architecture has to guarantee that one tenant's credentials and data can never reach another tenant's session — at any layer.

This guide covers the core architectural patterns for multi-tenant integrations: credential isolation, per-user connection routing, connection lifecycle management, and scaling considerations. The implementation examples use viaSocket's Integration Layer, which handles OAuth and token storage across 2,300+ apps.

The Multi-Tenant Integration Problem

A single-tenant integration is straightforward: one set of credentials, one OAuth token, one API client. A multi-tenant integration multiplies every concern:

  • Credential isolation: Each tenant's OAuth tokens must be stored and retrieved independently. A lookup error that returns the wrong tenant's token is a data breach.
  • Connection state: Each tenant has their own set of connected apps, which can be connected, disconnected, or re-authenticated independently.
  • Routing: When your backend triggers an action (send a Slack message, create a HubSpot contact), the action must use the correct tenant's credentials, not a shared pool.
  • Scale: Token refresh, re-authentication prompts, and connection health checks must work reliably across thousands of tenants simultaneously.

Building all of this from scratch — per integration, per provider — is the main reason integration development is consistently underestimated.

The Core Pattern: Identifier-Scoped Credential Storage

The foundation of any multi-tenant integration architecture is a stable, unique identifier per tenant that scopes all credential storage and retrieval.

In viaSocket's model, this is the unique_identifier field in the JWT payload:

const payload = {
  org_id: process.env.VIASOCKET_ORG_ID,
  project_id: process.env.VIASOCKET_PROJECT_ID,
  unique_identifier: tenantId
};

const token = jwt.sign(payload, process.env.VIASOCKET_EMBED_SECRET, {
  algorithm: 'HS256',
  expiresIn: '1h'
});

Every OAuth token viaSocket stores is keyed to this identifier. When your backend requests an action execution for a given unique_identifier, viaSocket retrieves only the credentials belonging to that identifier. Cross-tenant credential access is structurally prevented at the storage layer.

Choosing your identifier: Use your internal tenant or user ID — a stable, immutable string that maps one-to-one to your tenants. Do not use email addresses (they can change), session tokens (they expire), or composite keys that might be reused.

Four Isolation Dimensions

1. Credential Isolation

Each tenant's OAuth tokens are stored under their unique_identifier. Two tenants who both connect Slack get separate token records. Revoking one tenant's connection leaves the other's untouched.

Your responsibility: ensure the unique_identifier in every JWT you sign is correct for the authenticated session. This is a backend concern — the JWT is signed server-side with your embed_secret and delivered to the frontend via a protected API endpoint.

Where this multi-tenant integration architecture differs from Merge.dev's per-customer OAuth is covered in the alternatives guide.

2. Connection State Isolation

Each tenant sees only their own connected apps. The SDK methods are automatically scoped to the unique_identifier from the initialisation token:

// Returns only the apps connected by this tenant
const enabled = await viasocket.user.findEnabled();

// Opens a connection flow scoped to this tenant
await viasocket.connect({ app: 'notion' });

There is no shared connection state across tenants. A tenant who disconnects an app affects only their own record.

3. Action Execution Routing

When your backend triggers an integration action, the unique_identifier in the request body tells viaSocket which tenant's credentials to use:

await fetch(`https://flow.sokt.io/func/${process.env.SCRIPT_ID}`, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    unique_identifier: tenantId,
    app: 'hubspot',
    action: 'create_contact',
    params: { email: contactEmail, firstname: firstName }
  })
});

The script_id in the URL identifies the workflow. The unique_identifier in the body selects the tenant's credentials. Both are required — neither alone is sufficient to execute a routed action.

4. Re-Authentication Isolation

OAuth tokens expire and get revoked. When a single tenant's connection breaks, only that tenant needs to re-authenticate. Your frontend can check connection health per-tenant and prompt re-authentication selectively, without affecting any other tenant's active connections.

Connection Lifecycle Management

A production multi-tenant integration needs to handle the full connection lifecycle, not just the happy path.

Initial connection: The tenant clicks Connect in your UI, the SDK opens the OAuth flow, viaSocket handles the token exchange, and the token is stored under the tenant's identifier.

Checking connection status: Before executing an action for a tenant, verify the connection exists:

const enabled = await viasocket.user.findEnabled();
const hasSlack = enabled.some(app => app.name === 'slack');

if (!hasSlack) {
  // Prompt the tenant to connect Slack before proceeding
}

Handling disconnection: Tenants can disconnect apps explicitly, or tokens can be revoked by the provider. Your integration logic should handle action failures gracefully and surface re-connection prompts rather than failing silently.

Tenant offboarding: When a tenant leaves your product, revoke and remove their connections. This is both a security practice and a hygiene requirement for maintaining clean credential records.

Scaling Considerations

Don't Store OAuth Tokens Yourself

The most common scaling mistake is duplicating token storage — pulling tokens from a managed OAuth layer and caching them in your own database. This creates two problems: your cache goes stale when tokens refresh, and you are now responsible for the security of credentials you did not need to hold.

If you are using a managed OAuth layer, let it own token storage. Your backend's job is to route requests with the correct unique_identifier, not to hold credentials.

Scope JWT Expiry Tightly

JWTs should have short expiry windows — one hour is a reasonable default. Return a fresh JWT from your backend at the start of each session rather than issuing long-lived tokens. Since the JWT generation is a lightweight signing operation, there is no meaningful performance cost to short expiry.

Keep Script IDs and Secrets in Environment Variables

Your embed_secret (the JWT signing key) and your script_id values are credentials. Store them in environment variables, rotate them if they are exposed, and never include them in client-side code.

AI Agent Integrations

If your product includes AI agent features, the same multi-tenant isolation model applies. When an agent executes a tool call on behalf of a tenant, the action execution must include that tenant's unique_identifier so the correct credentials are used. Do not share a single agent credential set across tenants for actions that operate on tenant-owned data.

Architecture Summary

Concern Responsibility How
Credential storage viaSocket (managed) Keyed to unique_identifier
JWT signing Your backend HS256 with embed_secret; secret never sent to client
Connection UI Your frontend + SDK SDK initialised with per-session JWT
Action execution Your backend POST to flow.sokt.io/func/script_id with unique_identifier
Tenant identifier accuracy Your backend Match JWT unique_identifier to authenticated session
Token refresh viaSocket (managed) Automatic per provider

  • How to Handle OAuth for Multi-Tenant SaaS Integrations with viaSocket

  • Developer Documentation

What Paragon Is Built For

Paragon manages the OAuth, the connector logic, and the integration runtime.

Where Teams Look for Alternatives

Teams typically look for Paragon alternatives when:

1. Integration breadth. Paragon's connector catalog covers common B2B SaaS categories well. Teams whose users connect to less common or long-tail apps sometimes find gaps that require custom connector development.

2. AI agent delivery model. Paragon's ActionKit provides MCP-based integration for AI agents. Teams that need multi-modal AI delivery — tool-calling endpoint, user-facing white-label MCP server, and webhook-triggered action sequences — from a single integration catalog sometimes need a broader deployment surface.

3. Pricing structure. Paragon offers a free self-serve start, with paid tiers that require sales engagement for exact rates. Teams that want fully published, self-serve pricing at production scale look for alternatives.

4. Deployment flexibility. Some teams need the embedded workflow builder, AI tool-calling, and webhook-triggered automation to share the same integration catalog — without maintaining separate infrastructure for each pattern.

Five-Criteria Comparison: viaSocket vs Paragon

1. Deployment Model

Paragon offers an embedded integration UI (white-labeled, inside your SaaS product), managed OAuth per user, and ActionKit for AI agent MCP integration. Self-hosting is available for teams with data residency requirements.

viaSocket offers three deployment models:

  • Embedded iPaaS — white-labeled visual workflow builder embedded in your SaaS, backed by 2,300+ app connectors
  • Actions for AI — AI agent tool-calling across 2,300+ apps with per-user managed OAuth
  • Actions via Webhook — backend webhook triggers multi-app action sequences

Paragon offers a free self-serve signup to start. Paid production rates are usage-based and require sales engagement for exact pricing. This is common for enterprise-grade embedded iPaaS platforms, but creates friction for teams that want to model costs before a sales call.

3. Integration Breadth

Paragon covers a curated connector catalog across common B2B SaaS categories. The catalog is strong for CRM, HRIS, support, and productivity tools. Exact connector counts are not prominently published — check useparagon.com for the current catalog.

viaSocket provides 2,300+ pre-built app integrations maintained by the platform — CRM, marketing, support, finance, HR, developer tools, communication, and more. See /features for the full catalog.

For teams whose customers use a predictable set of enterprise tools, Paragon's curated approach may be sufficient. For teams needing broader coverage across less common apps, viaSocket's catalog breadth is an advantage.

4. AI/MCP Readiness

Paragon offers ActionKit — a server-side tool-calling layer that exposes your Paragon-managed integrations to AI agents. Paragon is investing actively in this area and ActionKit is a first-class product feature.

  • Actions for AI — 2,300+ app actions available as tool calls for your AI agent, with per-user OAuth scoped to your SaaS tenant model

posts.title: Webhook Triggers in viaSocket: Technical Implementation Guide
posts.description: A technical guide to receiving and processing inbound webhooks in viaSocket: how to configure a webhook trigger, retrieve your endpoint URL, validate payloads, and build reliable event-driven workflows.
posts.author: Abhijeet Singh
posts.html:
Webhooks let external services push events directly to your viaSocket workflows the moment something happens — a payment completes, a form is submitted, a record changes. Instead of polling an API, your workflow waits and reacts.

This guide explains how to set up a webhook trigger in viaSocket, get your inbound endpoint URL, validate incoming payloads, and handle events reliably.

How Inbound Webhooks Work in viaSocket

Every workflow in viaSocket can start with a webhook trigger. When you add a webhook trigger step, viaSocket generates a unique endpoint URL for that workflow. Any HTTP POST to that URL fires the workflow with the posted payload as the trigger data.

The pattern is:

  1. You create a workflow and add a webhook trigger
  2. viaSocket gives you a unique endpoint URL
  3. You register that URL with the external service (Stripe, GitHub, your own app, etc.)
  4. The external service POSTs events to the URL
  5. viaSocket executes the workflow with the event payload

Getting Your Webhook Endpoint URL

The endpoint URL is generated when you add a webhook trigger to a workflow. The URL follows this format:

https://flow.viasocket.com/webhook/{token}

where {token} is a unique identifier tied to that workflow. You can find the URL in the trigger step configuration inside the workflow editor. Copy it and paste it into the external service's webhook settings.

Each workflow gets its own distinct URL. If you need to handle events from multiple services, create a separate workflow for each source.

Validating Incoming Payloads

Most webhook senders include a signature header so you can verify the request is genuine and has not been tampered with. How you handle this in viaSocket depends on the sender.

Using a Custom Code Step for Signature Verification

For services that sign their payloads (Stripe uses a Stripe-Signature header with HMAC-SHA256; GitHub uses X-Hub-Signature-256; others follow similar patterns), the reliable approach in viaSocket is to add a code step immediately after the webhook trigger.

In that code step:

  1. Read the raw request body and the signature header from the trigger data
  2. Recompute the expected signature using the shared secret the service gave you
  3. Compare the computed signature against the received header using a constant-time comparison
  4. Return an error or stop the workflow if the signatures do not match

This approach works for any signing scheme and gives you full control over the validation logic. It is the recommended pattern until viaSocket publishes confirmed native signature verification settings for specific sources.

Filtering by IP Allowlist

Some services publish a list of IP addresses their webhooks originate from. If the service you are integrating with provides one, you can add a filter step that checks the source IP against the allowlist as a secondary control. This is a defence-in-depth measure, not a replacement for signature verification.

Handling Event Payloads

The entire POST body is available as trigger data in your workflow steps. You can reference any field in subsequent steps using viaSocket's variable picker.

A few practical considerations:

  • Most services send JSON. viaSocket parses the body automatically and makes fields accessible as named variables.
  • Some services send form-encoded data. Check the sender's documentation and parse accordingly in a code step if needed.
  • If the sender retries on non-2xx responses, make your workflow idempotent where possible — processing the same event twice should not create duplicate side effects.

Responding to the Sender

viaSocket returns a 200 response to the sender as soon as the webhook is received. Workflow execution happens after acknowledgement. This means:

  • The sender gets a fast acknowledgement and will not time out waiting for your workflow to finish
  • If your workflow fails partway through, the sender has already received its 200 and will not automatically retry unless it has its own retry logic

For critical workflows, log incoming events at the trigger step so you have a record independent of whether downstream steps succeed.

Reliability and Retries

viaSocket retries failed workflow steps automatically when a downstream action fails due to a temporary error. This covers failures in action steps (writing to a CRM, sending a message) but not the initial webhook receipt — once viaSocket has acknowledged the POST, the event is in the system.

The exact retry count and backoff schedule are not currently published in the public documentation. For high-stakes workflows where you need specific delivery guarantees, contact viaSocket support.

Common Setup Mistakes

Registering the wrong URL

Double-check the URL you paste into the external service. A single character difference means events go nowhere. Test with a sample payload immediately after registering.

Not activating the workflow

A workflow must be active to receive events. A draft or paused workflow will not process incoming webhooks even if the URL is correct.

Skipping payload validation

Without signature verification, anyone who discovers your webhook URL can POST arbitrary data and trigger your workflow. Always validate signatures for production workflows connected to external services.

Assuming synchronous execution

viaSocket acknowledges the webhook immediately and runs the workflow asynchronously. Do not design your integration to depend on a result returned in the HTTP response body.

FAQ

What is the inbound webhook URL format?

It follows the format https://flow.viasocket.com/webhook/{token}, where {token} is unique to the workflow. Find the full URL in the webhook trigger step inside your workflow editor.

Can I use the same webhook URL for multiple services?

Technically yes, but it is not recommended. Use separate workflows with separate URLs for each source so you can apply source-specific validation and routing logic independently.

How do I verify a Stripe or GitHub webhook signature?

viaSocket does not currently have confirmed native signature verification toggles for specific sources. The recommended approach is a custom code step immediately after the webhook trigger, where you recompute the expected signature and compare it against the header the sender provides.

What happens if my workflow fails after viaSocket acknowledges the webhook?

viaSocket retries failed action steps automatically. However, the sender has already received its 200 acknowledgement and will not re-send the event. Log trigger data at the start of your workflow so you can replay events manually if needed.

Does viaSocket support webhook authentication headers?

You can add filter or code steps that inspect any header included in the incoming request. For standard signing schemes, use a code step to perform the verification as described above.
